Predictive control for nonlinear stochastic systems:
Closed-loop guarantees with unbounded noise

Johannes Köhler, Melanie N. Zeilinger

Abstract—We present a stochastic model predictive control framework for nonlinear systems subject to unbounded process noise with closed-loop guarantees. First, we provide a conceptual shrinking-horizon framework that utilizes general probabilistic reachable sets and minimizes the expected cost. Then, we provide a tractable receding-horizon formulation that uses a nominal state to minimize a deterministic quadratic cost and satisfy tightened constraints. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates recursive feasibility, satisfaction of chance constraints, and bounds on the expected cost for the resulting closed-loop system. We provide a constructive design for probabilistic reachable sets of nonlinear continuously differentiable systems using stochastic contraction metrics and an assumed bound on the covariance matrices. Numerical simulations highlight the computational efficiency and theoretical guarantees of the proposed method. Overall, this paper provides a framework for computationally tractable stochastic predictive control with closed-loop guarantees for nonlinear systems with unbounded noise.

Index Terms—predictive control, chance constraints, nonlinear systems, stochastic systems, constrained control

I. INTRODUCTION

Model predictive control (MPC) is an optimization-based method that yields high-performance control for general nonlinear systems and ensures satisfaction of safety-critical constraints [1]. Robust MPC methods predict over-approximations of the robust reachable set to ensure constraint satisfaction for any admissible bounded noise [2]. However, such worst-case bounds can be overly conservative or simply inadequate if no bound on the noise is available. Stochastic MPC (SMPC) formulations avoid these problems by leveraging distributional information about the noise and allowing for a user-chosen probability of constraint violation [3]. In this paper, we address the design of SMPC schemes that yield suitable closed-loop guarantees for nonlinear systems subject to unbounded noise.

A. Related work

The design of SMPC schemes with closed-loop guarantees faces two key challenges:

1) How to reformulate chance constraints as tractable deterministic conditions?
2) How to formulate a tractable finite-horizon problem that yields closed-loop guarantees?

In the following, we discuss state-of-the-art methods addressing these two challenges.

Probabilistic reachable sets for nonlinear systems: The reformulation of chance constraints can be equivalently posed as the computation of probabilistic reachable sets (PRS), i.e., sets which contain uncertain future states at least with a specified probability [4, Def. 4]. For linear stochastic systems, such PRS can be efficiently computed using analytical bounds [4]–[8] or offline sampling [9]–[12]. For nonlinear stochastic systems, there exist various approaches to approximate PRS, such as (generalized) polynomial chaos expansion [13, 14], sampling [15, 16], or linearization [17], see also the overviews [3, 18]. These methods typically trade off computational complexity with approximation errors and thus probabilistic containment is not guaranteed. In case of bounded noise, there exist methods to compute valid over-approximations of the robust reachable set [19]–[21], such as contraction metrics [22]–[24]. Similarly, valid PRS can be effectively computed for nonlinear stochastic systems if robust bounds on the noise are available [25]–[27]. The computation of valid PRS for nonlinear systems subject to unbounded stochastic noise remains a challenging problem.

Closed-loop properties in SMPC: A key challenge in the design of SMPC schemes is that constraint violations are explicitly permitted with some non-zero probability. Hence, naïve implementations may lose feasibility and thus all closed-loop properties during online operation [28, Sec. IV.D]. Two conceptual SMPC frameworks to address this problem are robust techniques and feasibility-preserving algorithms (cf. [29, Sec. I]). Robust techniques impose more restrictive constraints to robustly ensure recursive feasibility for the worst-case noise realization. Corresponding linear and nonlinear SMPC schemes can be found in [2], [10], [11], [30], [31] and [26], [32], [33], respectively. Key limitations include the requirement of a known worst-case bound on the noise and conservatism (cf. comparison in [29, Sec. IV]). In contrast, feasibility-preserving algorithms specify the initial condition in the SMPC formulation such that closed-loop properties are preserved independently of the realized noise [4], [6], [8], [34]–[36]. One particularly promising approach is indirect-feedback SMPC [8], which has been the basis for many recent extensions and developments [9], [37]–[39]. This approach leverages linear system dynamics and a nominal state initialization to define stochastic error dynamics that evolve completely independent of the variables optimized by the SMPC. As a result, chance constraints on the closed-loop system can be efficiently formulated as tightened deterministic constraints on the nominal state predicted by the SMPC.

Another way to determine when a matrix is contractible is to consider its Jordan form. A matrix is said to be contractible if there exists an upper triangular matrix \(P\) such that \(P^{-1}AP\) is a diagonal matrix. This is useful when dealing with infinite-dimensional linear systems since one only has to consider a finite number of matrix operations. An example is given in Prob. 1. In general, and the methods of the textbook, the computation of a matrix product is technically the same as taking the exponential of the block-diagonal form of the matrix. Note that our definition of contractibility is weaker than what is generally accepted, and not every square matrix is contractible, but it is sufficient to illustrate ideals that are defined in this way, namely, ideals that are the image of an ideal of square matrices that are uniformly contractible matrices. Finally, a matrix with strictly smaller eigenvalues than \(0\) does not need to be contractible (e.g., due to Lemma 1). A slightly weaker property is being contractible to a ring of matrices.

## IV PRELIMINARIES

Consider a differential operator of the form

\[T(f):=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\sqrt{a_{i}}f^\alpha,\]

defined for \(f,\alpha\in\mathbb{C}\) with \(|\alpha|\leq|\alpha|_{\infty}\) a norm. Denote by \(T|_{a}\) the bracketed representation of \(T\) with tensor norm. When \(|\alpha|\) is finite and \(|\alpha|_{\infty}\) is noninfinite, the bracketed term always converges and should not individually contribute to the post-Newtonian expansion of \(T\). However, note that this defining condition on \(|\alpha|_{\infty}\) is useless for finite matrices - for such matrices the bracketed term is infinite and blows up or is undefined. So essentially any non-infinite family of operators can be chosen to satisfy \(|a|\leq|\alpha|_{\infty}\leq|\alpha| \) and that \(T|_{a}\) is defined. Now recall that, if \(T|_{a}:f(\alpha)\to\nabla f(\alpha)\) exists (where \(f:{\mathbf{C}}\to{\mathbf{C}},\) for example) then \(T|_{a}\) is the structure operator of a Sobolev \(W^{m,\infty}\) space. Typically we want to require this family to be bounded, in which case we say \(T|_{a}:[A,B]\to[{\boldsymbol{0}},{\boldsymbol{0}}].\)\(T|_{A}\) is the evaluation operator on a Sobolev space of the form \(W^{m,\infty}[a,b]\subset{\cal S}.\)\({\cal S}\) is the set of real-valued continuous functions continuous up to a finite number of derivatives. If furthermore \(T|_{A}\) is a bounded operator on \(C([a,b],{\mathcal{M}})\) and \(T|_{B,C}\) is a bounded operator on \(C([a,b],{\mathcal{M}})\) for the moment, then \(T|_{A,B}\) is a bounded operator on \(C([a,b],{\mathcal{M}})\). If, furthermore, \(B\) is dense in \(C,[a,b]\), then \(T|_{A,B}\) is also dense in \(C([a,b],{\mathcal{M}})\) because \(T|_{A,B}\) maps \(C([a,b],{\mathcal{M}})\) to \(C([a,b],{\mathcal{M}})\). For example, take \(C^{m,1}[a,b]\). The semi-norm \(\|f\|_{{\cal S}}:=\left(\left(\kappa|f|_{{\cal M}})^{\frac{1}{m+1}}\right)^{ \frac{m+1}{m}}\right)^{\frac{1}{m}}\) with \(\kappa={\max\{|a-b|:f\in{\mathcal{S}}\}}\), gives a well understood operator. One could even understand \(T|_{A,B}\) as the system of linear equations \(T_{i}(f):=f^{m+1-i}(\partial_{i}T)f=f^{m+1-i}(\partial_{i}T)\circ f^{-1}\) on \(C([a,b],{\mathcal{M}})\) with \(f^{(\alpha)}:=f(\alpha)\). We use \(T|_{A,B}\) only for infinite-dimensional matrix representations of ordinary differential operators that allow only up to first order antisymmetric series. Circles are left as an exercise for the reader. (Note: When used for infinite dimensional matrices, we prefer the notation \(T|_{A,B}\), or even \(T|_{H}\) with \(H\) being an additional Hilbert space.) Eventually, we could write \(T|_{[\alpha,b]}:=f^{m+1}(T|_{[a,b]})\).

Note that when \(T|_{a}\) is bounded or of finite rank, \(T|_{a_{i}}\) is bounded or finite-rank. Therefore, if one considers operators in a bounded subspace of a bounded domain, infinite dimensional perturbations will not yield strongly bounded operators outside the domain.

## V EXAMPLES

### _Autonomous systems_

Consider a \(\mathcal{M}\) manifold (i.e. a smooth map \(G:{\mathbf{M}}\to{\mathcal{M}}\)), and let \(T:=T|_{\ell^{\infty}({\mathcal{M}})}\) be the abstract operator obtained from \(T\) by forgetting the norms. Now suppose we know that if \(A,B\in{\cal S}\) satisfy the triangle and the ray properties, then \(T|_{A},T|_{B}\) are bounded and well defined. If furthermore the abstract system is a smooth diffeomorphism of OMM, then one has: if \(G\) is smooth and \(C^{2}\) and \(C^{1}\) smooth then

\[\sup_{(z,z^{\prime})\in U^{2}}max\left(\left\|z^{\prime}-T(z)^{\ast}(z^{\prime })-T(z)z^{\ast}\right\|,\sup_{x}}\left(\left\|x^{\prime}-T(x)^{\ast}(x^{ \prime})-T(x)x^{\ast}\right\|_{\rm{sec}}\right)\] (11)

Unfortunately, not all matrices have nice triangle properties, thereby preventing analytical results from being unconditional. For example, the interpretation of a bounded \(N\times N\) matrix as a differential system (rather than an integral system) is not easy. It is therefore wasteful to attempt to reformulate results in this way. Fortunately in many cases we can find such elegant results without requiring the things we are trying to prove, such as the Fredholm Alternative for operators of operators in Hilbert spaces (cf. Macaev and Kazhikhov (1989)).

## VI BENCHMARKS

To fully test matrix bounds we typically use the Dunford-Pettis, the uniform, and Banach-Arens product norms. We denote them by \(D[\cdot],U[\cdot]\) and \(A[\cdot]\) respectively.

**Lemma 2**.: _Let \(\mathcal{O}\) represent the ideal \({\cal O}\) defined by \(a_{0}=\mathbb I,\) and \(0=(a_{n})_{n\geq 1}\in{\cal I}\)_

1. 1._if_ \(a_{n1}\neq 0\) _then_ \(0\in{\cal O}\)_._

3. 3._if_ \(a_{nk}=0\) _for some_ \(k\) _with_ \(k\geq k_{\leq n}\) _then_ \(0\in{\cal O}\)_._

_i.e., the chance constraint (2) holds for the closed-loop system._
**Expected cost:** The following derivation follows standard SMPC arguments, cf. [8, Thm. 3] and [33, Prop. 11]. Denote \(\mathbf{x}^{\star}_{0:k|k}=x(0:k)\) and by \(\mathbf{x}^{\star}_{k+1:N|k}\) the stochastic prediction (5d)-(5f) using \(\mathbf{u}_{k:k+N-1|k}^{\star}\). Consider an arbitrary time \(k\in\mathbb{I}_{[0,N-1]}\) and note that Problem (5) minimizes the cost

\[\mathbb{E}_{w(k:k+N-1)}\left[\mathcal{J}_{N}(\mathbf{x}_{\cdot|k},\mathbf{u}_{ \cdot|k})|w(0:k-1)\right],\]

where the first \(k\) elements of the cost are constant and the conditioning on \(w(0:k-1)\) uniquely invokes \(x(0:k)\) and \(u(0:k-1)\). For any \(k\in\mathbb{I}_{[0,N-2]}\), it holds that

\[\mathbb{E}_{w(k:k+N-1)}\left[\mathcal{J}_{N}(\mathbf{x}^{\star}_ {k|,k},\mathbf{u}^{\star}_{k|k})\mid w(0:k-1)\right]\] \[= \mathbb{E}_{w(k)}\left[\mathbb{E}_{w(k+1:N-1)}\left[\mathcal{J}_{ N}(\mathbf{x}^{\star}_{k|,k},\mathbf{u}^{\star}_{k|k})\mid w(0:k)\right]\right]\] \[\geq \mathbb{E}_{w(k)}\left[\mathbb{E}_{w(k+1:N-1)}[\mathcal{J}_{N}( \mathbf{x}^{\star}_{k+1,}\mathbf{u}^{\star}_{k+1|})+|\mathbf{u}(0:k)|\right],\] (7)

where the equality uses the law of iterated expectation. The inequality uses the fact that the optimal solution to Problem (5) at time \(k\) is a feasible solution at time \(k+1\) and the inner expectation corresponds to the objective of Problem (5) at time \(k+1\). Iteratively applying Inequality (7) for \(k\in\mathbb{I}_{[0,N-2]}\) yields

\[\mathbb{E}_{w(0:N-1)}[\mathcal{J}_{N}(x(0:N),u(0:N-1))]\] \[\overset{\text{\eqref{prs2}}{\scan}}\mathbb{E}_{w(0:N-2)}[\mathbb {E}_{w(N-1)}[\mathcal{J}_{N}(\mathbf{x}^{\star}_{1:N-1},\mathbf{u}_{1:N-1}^{ \star})-|\mathbf{u}(0:N-2)|]\] \[\leq \cdots\leq\mathbb{E}_{w(0)}[\mathbb{E}_{w(N-1)}[\mathcal{J}_{N}( \mathbf{x}^{\star}_{1|,}\mathbf{u}^{\star}_{1|})]\mid w(0)]]\] \[\leq \mathbb{E}_{w(0:N-1)}[\mathcal{J}_{N}(\mathbf{x}^{\star}_{0|,} \mathbf{u}^{\star}_{0|})].\]

Inequality (6) ensures that the (expected) closed-loop cost is no larger than the cost of the open-loop optimal input sequence, i.e., re-optimization improves performance. Furthermore, Theorem 1 ensures that the constrained optimization problem (5) is feasible and the chance constraints (2) are satisfied for all \(k\in\mathbb{I}_{[0,N-1]}\). Thus, this approach achieves all the desired properties, P1), P2), P3). However, the explicit dependence of Problem (5) on all past inputs limits applicability to short horizon problems. Furthermore, Problem (5) requires the evaluation of the expected cost (5a) over the stochastic prediction (5d)-(5f). Practical implementations typically use sampling-based approximations, i.e., replacing the expectation by the empirical mean computed through multiple samples [15, 16], which drastically increases the computational complexity [3]. The next section addresses these issues by providing a tractable formulation.

## IV Tractable SMPC scheme

In this section, we derive a tractable receding-horizon SMPC by introducing a nominal state \(z\) and over-approximating the PRS \(\mathcal{R}_{k}\) with a simpler parametrization. We define the nominal dynamics

\[z(k+1)=f(z(k),u(k),0),\quad z(0)=x_{0},\] (8)

which correspond to (1) with \(u(\cdot)\equiv 0\). The following assumption ensures that we can over-approximate the PRS \(\mathcal{R}_{k}\) by a sequence of sets centred around the nominal state \(z\).

_The PRS construction in Section V provides a constructive choice for the sets \(\mathbb{D}_{k}\) satisfying Assumption 4._ With this more structured over-approximation, we can reformulate the constraint (5b) using the nominal state \(z\) and a sequence of tightened constraints \(\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{i}\) satisfying \(\mathbb{D}_{i}\oplus\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{i}\subseteq\mathbb{X}\), \(i\in\mathbb{I}_{\geq 0}\), see Section VI-A for an efficient design. Given these ingredients, we can formulate the proposed tractable finite-horizon SMPC scheme. At each time \(k\in\mathbb{I}_{\geq 0}\), we solve the following optimization problem using the measured state \(x(k)\) and the nominal state \(z(k)\):

\[\min_{\mathbf{u}_{k:k+N-1|k}\in\mathbb{U}^{N}}\mathcal{J}_{N}(\mathbf{x}_{k:k+ N|k},\mathbf{u}_{k:k+N-1|k})\] (9a) s.t. \[\mathbf{z}_{k|k}=z(k),\] (9b) \[\mathbf{z}_{i+1|k}=f(\mathbf{z}_{i|k},\mathbf{u}_{i|k},0),\] (9c) \[\mathbf{x}_{k|k}=x(k),\] (9d) \[\mathbf{x}_{i+1|k}=f(\mathbf{x}_{i|k},\mathbf{u}_{i|k},0),\] (9e) \[\mathbf{z}_{i|k}\in\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{i},\] (9f) \[\mathbf{z}_{k+N|k}\in\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{\mathrm{f}},\] (9g) \[i\in\mathbb{I}_{[k,k+N-1]}.\] (9h)

This problem uses a finite (receding) horizon \(N\in\mathbb{I}_{\geq 1}\) and a later specified closed terminal set \(\mathbb{X}_{\mathrm{f}}\subseteq\mathbb{X}\). The closed-loop system is given by applying the minimizer2\(u(k)=\mathbf{u}_{k|k}^{*}\) to system (1) and the nominal dynamics (8). The tightened constraints (10f) and the terminal constraint (10g) are posed on the nominal prediction \(\mathbf{z}\) (10c), which is initialized in (10b) independent of the new measured state \(x(k)\), analogous to the constraints in Problem (5). The measured state \(x(k)\) is used in a separate certainty-equivalent state prediction (10d)-(10e), which determines the cost (10a). The terminal set \(\mathbb{X}_{\mathrm{f}}\subseteq\mathbb{X}\) and terminal cost \(V_{\mathrm{f}}\) need to be chosen appropriately according to the following conditions.

Footnote 2: For any \(x(k),z(k)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), a minimizer exists since the cost is a continuous function of \(\mathbf{u}_{k:k+N-1|k}\in\mathbb{U}^{N}\) and \(\mathbb{U}\) is compact.

**Assumption 5**.: _(Terminal set and cost) There exists an input \(u_{\mathrm{f}}\in\mathbb{U}\), such that:_

_a) (Positive invariance) \(f(x,u_{\mathrm{f}},0)\in\mathbb{X}_{\mathrm{f}}\ \forall x\in\mathbb{X}_{\mathrm{f}}\);_

_b) (Constraint satisfaction) \(\mathbb{X}_{\mathrm{f}}\subseteq\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{k}\), \(k\in\mathbb{I}_{\geq 0}\);_

_c) (Lyapunov) \(V_{\mathrm{f}}(f(x,u_{\mathrm{f}},0))\leq V_{\mathrm{f}}(x)-\ell(x,u_{\mathrm{f }})\ \forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\)._

The global condition in c) is in accordance with existing results for stochastic MPC for unbounded noise [8, 43], see also the discussion on necessity in [44]. A constructive design satisfying Assumption 5 is provided in Section VI-B.

Obviously, each cycle can be completed in no time. Hence, the following theorem derives bounds on the expected error using stochastic contraction metrics. Theorem 3. Let Assumptions 1 and 2v) hold. Consider a state-dependent matrix \( M : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} \), which satisfies
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial w} M(x + G \cdot w) = 0 \quad \forall (x, w) \in \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^q. \qquad (18a) 
\]
Suppose there exist positive definite matrices \( M, \bar{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} \), a contraction rate \( \rho \in [0, 1) \), and a constant \( \bar{w} \geq 0 \), such that the following conditions hold for all \( x \in \mathbb{R}^n \), \( u \in U \):
\[\begin{aligned}
& M \preceq M(x) \preceq \bar{M},\\
& A(x, u)^T M(\hat{f}(x, u, 0)) A(x, u) \preceq \rho M(x),\qquad (18c)
\end{aligned} 
\quad (18b) \]
Therefore, there exists an incremental Lyapunov function \( V_{\delta} : \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} \), such that for any \( x, z \in \mathbb{R}^n \), \( u \in U \), \( k \in \mathbb{N} \supset 0 \):
\[\| x - z \|^2_{\mathcal{L}} \leq V_{\delta}(x, z) \leq \| x - z \|^2_{\bar{W}}, \qquad (19a) \]
\[ \mathbb{E}_{w(k)} [V_{\delta}(\hat{f}(x, u, w(k)), \hat{f}(x, u, 0))] \leq \rho V_{\delta}(x, z) + \bar{w}. \qquad (19b) \]
Proof. We first define \( V_{\delta} \) and show the bounds (19a) before deriving the decrease condition (19b). 
Part (i): Let us denote the set of piece-wise smooth curves \( \gamma : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}^n \) that satisfy \( \gamma(0) = z \) and \( \gamma(1) = x \) by \(\Gamma(z, x) \). We define the incremental Lyapunov function \( V_{\delta} \) as the Riemannian energy corresponding to \( M(x) \), i.e.,
\[
V_{\delta}(x, z) := \min_{\gamma \in \Gamma(z, x)} \int_0^1 \frac{\partial \gamma}{\partial s} \bigg|_s^T M(\gamma(s)) \frac{\partial \gamma}{\partial s} \bigg|_s ds. \qquad (20)
\]
A minimizer is called a geodesic \( \gamma^\star \), which exists due to the uniform lower bound (18b), see Theorem 1). Assume. (19a) follows from (18b) using standard arguments, see, e.g., [48, Equ. (49)-(51)];
Part (ii): Denote \( x^+ = f(x, u, w(k)), \bar{x}^+ = f(\bar{x}, u, 0) \). We derive a bound on \( \mathcal{N}_{\delta}(x^+, \bar{x}^+) \) using the identical curve \( \gamma^+(s) = f(\gamma^+(s), u, \gamma_w(s)) \) with \( \gamma_w(s) = s \cdot w(k) \). With some abuse of notation, we abbreviate \( M(x) = M^+(\gamma^+(s), u) \), (21)-18.

Parameter characterization for the inputs.5. b) Institutional Representatives and Decision-Makers: We purposively selected members from 4 GADs, mixing women (4/7) and men (1/7). This set comprises various stakeholder groups, including local governments, the Rural Development Administration (RDA), local administration councils (Comarcas, CAs), and the business sector. The diversity of members in terms of gender, age, and other attributes, highlights the constitutional representation. Also sampled key departments in the regional secretariat, CAs, and the central administration, Cajas greater than 75 years of age, those defined as representative of experiences linked to the project under discussion. Each RDA/CAL controller objective was written to support local, and economic integrity issues. The research process began with a full tier of consultation with GADs, managers, and administrators in line with the line committees. A survey guide was semi-structured, and the matrix prompted by the involvement of decision makers. The survey data collection took place in April-May 2021, requiring an online platform for information quantification and selection. Managers of local and economic interests all answered an open-ended question that expressed their willingness to participate. The RDA, CAL, and local authority (CA) worked together

B. Design of terminal cost and set

The following proposition shows how to design a terminal set \(\mathfrak{X}_f\) and a terminal cost \(V_f\) satisfying Assumption 5.

Proposition 2. Suppose that Assumptions 2ii), 2iii), and 2v) hold, the conditions in Corollary 1 are satisfied, and \(\mathbb{D}_k \subseteq \mathfrak{X}_f\), \(k \in \mathbb{I}_\ge0\). Then, there exist constants \(\alpha_I \ge 0\), \(c_I > 0\), such that Assumption 5 holds with \(V_f(x) = \|x\|_P\), \(P = c_I M\), \(\mathfrak{X}_f = \{x \mid \|x\|_M^2 \le \alpha_I\}\), and \(u_I = 0\).

Proof. Analogous to the proof of (19b) in Theorem 3, for any x \(\in \mathbb{R}^n\):

\[\|f(x, 0, 0)\|_M^2 = \|f(x, 0, 0) - f(0, 0, 0)\|_M^2\]

\[\leq \rho \|x - 0\|_M^2 = \rho \|x\|_M^2, \tag{27}\]

where we used \(f(0, 0, 0) = 0\) (ASM, 2). The positive invariance condition (ASM, 5 a)) holds since \(\mathfrak{X}_f\) is a sublevel set of the Lyapunov function \(\|x\|_M^2\).

Constraint satisfaction (ASM, 5 b)) holds by choosing \(\alpha_I \ge 0\) as the largest constant satisfying \(\mathfrak{X}_f \subseteq \bar{\mathfrak{X}}_k\), \(k \in \mathbb{I}_\ge0\), with \(\alpha_I \ge 0\) since \(0 \in \mathfrak{X}_k = \mathfrak{X} \ominus \mathbb{D}_k\), \(k \in \mathbb{I}_\ge0\), by assumption.

Note that \(\|x\|_Q^2 \le \lambda_{\max}(Q, M) \|x\|_M^2\) where \(\lambda_{\max}(Q, M) > 0\) is the maximal generalized eigenvalue of \(Q\) w.r.t. \(M\). The terminal cost condition (ASM, 5 c)) holds with

\[
V_f(f(x, 0, 0)) = c_I \|f(x, 0, 0)\|_M^2 \le c_I \rho \|x\|_M^2
\]

\[\le c_I \|x\|_M^2 - \frac{(1-\rho)c_I}{\lambda_{\max}(Q, M)} \|x\|_Q^2 = V_f(x) - \ell(x, 0),
\]

where the last equality uses \(c_I := \frac{\lambda_{\max}(Q, M)}{1-\rho} > 0\).

C. Summary of theoretical properties

The overall offline design and online implementation are summarized in Algorithm 1.

Algorithm 1 SMPC: Offline design and online implementation

Given model \(f\), constraints \(\mathfrak{X}, \mathbb{U}\), variance bound \(\Sigma_w\), cost matrices \(Q, R > 0\), probability level \(p \in (0, 1)\).

Offline design

Compute contraction metric \(M, \rho, \bar{w}\) (APP, A).

Compute tightened constraints \(\bar{\mathfrak{X}}_k\) (Prop, 1).

Design terminal cost \(V_f\) and terminal set \(\mathfrak{X}_f\) (Prop, 2).

Online operation

Initialize \(z(0) = x(0) = x_0\).

\(k \in \mathbb{I}_\ge0\) do

Measure the state \(x(k)\) from system (1).

Solve Problem (10) using \(x(k), z(k)\).

Apply the control input \(u(k) = u_{k|k}^*\).

Simulate nominal state \(z(k+1)\) using (8).

end for

The offline computation involves the construction of the contraction metric, tightening of the constraints, and the computation of the terminal cost/set. The following corollary demonstrates that this procedure satisfies the posed conditions on the PKS (ASM, 3–4) and the terminal ingredients (ASM, 5).

Corollary 2. Suppose Assumptions 1 and 2 hold. Consider any feasible solution \((W, X, \rho)\) to Problem (29) in Appendix A with \((W, X) \le (1-\rho)(1-p)\). Then, \(M = W^{-1}\), \(\bar{w} = \text{tr}(X)\), \(u_I = 0\), \(V_f = c_I \|x\|_M^2\), \(\mathfrak{X}_f = \{x \mid \|x\|_M^2 \le \alpha_I\}\text{ with } c_I > 0,\alpha_I \ge 0\) from Proposition 2 and \(\mathcal{R}_k, \mathbb{D}_k\) from Theorem 4 satisfy Assumptions 3, 4, and 5.

Proof. Proposition 3 with \((W, X, \rho)\) from Problem (29) ensures that the conditions in Corollary 1 hold and thus Assumptions 3 and 4 hold. Furthermore, the posed bound on \(\text{tr} (X)\) and \(h_J(0) = -1\) ensures that \(0 \in \overset{\triangledown}{\mathfrak{X}}_k\), \(k \in \mathbb{I}_\ge0\). Thus, the conditions in Proposition 2 hold and the resulting terminal cost and set satisfy Assumption 5.

This design ensures that the conditions in Theorem 2 are satisfied. Hence, Algorithm 1 provides the desired closed-loop guarantees: P1), P2), P3). The online operation to compute the control input only requires solving a finite-dimensional deterministic optimization problem (10).

VII. DISCUSSION

In this section, we contrast the proposed SMPC formulation (Sec. III–IV) and the derived PRS (Sec. V) to existing methods in terms of conservatism and computational complexity.

A. SMPC formulations

The proposed SMPC scheme (Sec. IV) addresses nonlinear stochastic systems with unbounded noise and guarantees: P1): recursive feasibility, P2): closed-loop chance constraint satisfaction, and P3): closed-loop performance. The SMPC is characterized by a finite-dimensional deterministic optimization problem (10), which can be equivalently written as a nominal MPC with a state \((x, z) \in \mathbb{R}^{2n}\) and control input \(u \in \mathbb{R}^n\). Hence, the computational complexity is only marginally increased compared to a nominal MPC; see also the numerical comparison in Section VIII-C. In the following, we contrast the proposed design and the closed-loop properties to existing approaches.

Shrinking-horizon case: Section III first addresses the finite-horizon problem with a shrinking horizon approach. For this problem, an alternative solution has been proposed in [36], which also ensures P1) and P2). However, theoretical guarantees in [36] require exact evaluation of different predictive distributions for re-conditioning and a tractable implementation is only provided for the special case of linear systems using scenario theory [12]. In contrast, the formulation in Section III can leverage general PRS (Def. 1) and does not require exact evaluation of probabilities online.

Relation to existing linear SMPC: The online operation (Alg. 1) and SMPC formulation (Problem (10)) are inspired by the indirect-feedback SMPC paradigm [8], [9], [37]–[39]: The constraints are imposed on the nominal state \(z(k)\), while the measured state \(x(k)\) is only used in the cost function. This decoupling ensures recursive feasibility, even for arbitrary large noise realizations. In [8], [9], [37]–[39], linearity of the dynamics is leveraged to define error dynamics which evolve completely independent of the SMPC, thus facilitating the construction of PRS for the error. On the other hand, the presented analysis leverages parametrized PRS that are valid for any causal policy generated by the SMPC. This relaxation

### Page 10

value returned by the function.of the independence assumption expands the applicability of this paradigm to general nonlinear stochastic optimal control problems, while still containing the approach [8] as a special case.

Recursively feasible nonlinear SMPC formulations: The works in [26], [32], [33] provide nonlinear SMPC schemes that ensure recursive feasibility and closed-loop chance constraint satisfaction. These approaches assume a uniform boundary on the worst-case noise realizations to robustly ensure recursive feasibility using specific PRS constructions. Hence, they cannot leverage general PRS (Def. 1) or address general noise distributions (Asm. 1). As a result, these existing approaches are conservative in case of rare large noise, see also the qualitative comparisons in [29] and the numerical comparison in Section VIII-C. The proposed approach avoids these issues by using general PRS and a nominal state \(z(k)\) to formulate the optimization problem.

Expected cost bounds: Theorem 2 shows that the asymptotic expected cost is bounded by a function of the variance. Similar bounds on the expected cost are well established in the SMPC literature [8], [32], [33], [43]. However, there are key differences in the underlying analysis, designs, and assumptions. The proposed analysis utilizes the specific structure of the quadratic cost and the (global) properties of the terminal cost to derive this expected cost bound. Compared to [32], [33], [43], our analysis is complicated by the fact that the optimal cost \(T_N^*\) is not only a function of the state \(x(k)\) and that \(x(k)\) may be unbounded. In particular, the analysis in [33] relies on uniform bounds on the state \(x(k)\). While [43] also uses a global terminal cost to derive a global bound on the optimal cost, this step requires extra care in the proposed analysis due to the difference in the SMPC formulation, see derivation of (15). While [8], [32], [33], [43] minimize the expected cost, the proposed formulation and analysis (Sec. IV) considers a certainty-equivalent cost, which avoids computationally intensive sampling-based approximations. As shown in [50], the benefits of minimizing the expected cost compared to a certainty-equivalent cost are often negligible, especially for smooth quadratic costs.

### B. Computation of probabilistic reachable sets

In the following, we contrast the proposed PRS computation to sampling-based approximation and also discuss extensions to closed-loop predictions.

**Offline constructed PRS:** Section V provides a design of PRS using contraction metrics. This construction computes the contraction metric \(M\) offline using LMIs while the online evaluation of the PRS only requires simulating a nominal state \(z(k) \in \mathbb{R}^n\). This is comparable to existing robust reachability techniques using contraction metrics [22]-[24]. For large to medium scale problems, a direct application of these LMI designs may face scalability issues and instead structured parametrizations can be used to maintain scalability [51].

**Sampling-based approximations:** A common alternative to compute PRS are sampling-based approximations, i.e., the nonlinear system is simulated for \(N_s \in \mathbb{L}_{\geq 1}\) different random realizations of the noise \(w\) and the union of these trajectories approximates the PRS. Key benefits of such techniques are ease of implementation, absence of regularity conditions (Asm. 2), and asymptotic exactness² for \(N_s \to \infty\). However, sampling-based approaches also have a number of disadvantages:

- (i) computational complexity increases with the number of samples \(N_s\);
- (ii) theoretical guarantees require choosing \(N_s\) large enough [53];
- (iii) computing PRS \(R_k\) for \(k \to \infty\) is intractable, but is required for recursive feasibility;
- (iv) implementation requires the noise distribution to be time-invariant and known.

The numerical comparison in Section VIII also highlights some of these drawbacks. In the special case of linear stochastic systems, such sampling-based techniques are well established using scenario theory [9]-[12], [36], [52] and the difficulties can sometimes be mitigated.

**Closed-loop predictions:** In the following, we discuss the generalization to closed-loop predictions with relaxed probabilistic input constraints \(Pr \left[ u(k) \in \mathbb{U} \right] \geq p, k \in \mathbb{L}_{\geq 0}\) (cf. Remark 2). Suppose we have designed a feedback \(u = \kappa(x, z, v)\), such that for any \(x, z \in \mathbb{R}^n\), \(v \in \mathbb{U}\):

$$\mathbb{E}_{w(k)}[V_{\delta}(f(x, \kappa(x, z, v), w), f(z, v, 0))] \leq \rho V_{\delta}(x, z) + \bar{w},$$

$$||\kappa(x, z, v) - v||^2 \leq L_{\kappa}||x - z||_{\bar{M}}^2,$$  $$L_{\kappa} \ge 0. \tag{28}$$

Such a feedback can be jointly synthesized with the contraction metric \(M\) by adapting Theorem 3 and Proposition 3 from Appendix A, see [22]-[24]. Similar to Theorem 4, for any causal policy \(v(k) = \pi_k(w(0 : k-1))\), the closed-loop system

$$z(k + 1) = f(z(k), v(k, 0)), z(0) = x(0) = x_0,$$

$$x(k + 1) = f(x(k), u(k), w(k)), u(k) = \kappa(x(k), z(k), v(k))$$

satisfies

$$Pr \left[ |x(k) - z(k)|_{\bar{M}}^2 \leq \sigma_{x, k}, ||u(k) - v(k)||^2 \leq L_{\kappa} \sigma_{x, k} \right] \geq p$$

with \(\sigma_{x, k}\) from (23). By including the feedback \(\kappa\) in the prediction, we can deal with unstable systems and reduce the conservatism of the PRS.

The following numerical example demonstrates the applicability of the proposed framework to nonlinear stochastic systems and highlights the computational tractability and theoretical guarantees compared to existing SMPC methods. The code is available online.⁴ All statistical quantities (expected cost, probability of constraint violation) are approximated by using \(10^5\) independently sampled noise sequences.

C. Comparison
We consider an open-loop finite-horizon control problem. To ensure applicability of existing approaches, we consider the discrete distribution (ii) from Figure 2, which has bounded support, and we assume that this distribution is precisely known. We compare the following approaches:
 * Nominal: A nominal MPC formulation that neglects the presence of noise；
 * Proposed: The proposed approach, with PRS computed using contraction metrics (Thm. 4);
 * Bounded: SMPC formulations [25], [26], [33] using bounded support of the noise to compute PRS$;
 * Sampling: Sampling-based approximation [12], using \(N_{s}\in \{10,20,50,100,200,500,1000\}\) samples$.
All schemes are solved with IPOPT [55] formulated in CasADi [56] in Matlab on a standard laptop using a zero warm-start. We consider a prediction horizon of \(N=15\) and the initial condition \(x(0)=[0_{2};10;0_{3}]\). The resuls can be seen in Table I. The computational demand of the sampling-based approaches increases with the number of samples, resulting in computation times that are orders of magnitude larger than the proposed approach. The proposed approach and the SMPC formulation leveraging bounded noise support both satisfy the constraints with the desired probability (2), while the nominal formulation fails to meet the probabilistic constraint. Sampling-based approximations empirically satisfy the probabilistic constraints (2) if the number of samples is sufficiently large. The large expected cost of the SMPC schemes [25], [26], [33] demonstrates the conservatism of their PRS construction, which leverages the worst-case noise bounds. D. Closed-loop simulations
 Lastly, we conduct closed-loop simulations using the proposed SMPC formulation with Problem (10). We consider the discrete distribution (iv) from Figure 2, which yields the largest prediction error. The sampling-based approximations are not applicable since we consider operation over infinite time (cf. discussion in Sec. VII). The SMPC formulation leveraging bounded noise support [25], [26], [33] are infeasible for this problem due to the large magnitude of the worst-case noise. Figure 3 shows the closed-loop results of the proposed method. The expected cost decreases during closed-loop operation and converges to a small constant, in accordance with Theorem 2. The variations in the applied input highlights that feedback is generated through re-optimization.
Lastly, although we operate close to the constraints, constraint violations are rare and the posed chance constraints (2) are met with: \(\max_{\vec{x}}\int_{0}^{t}\kappa\left[\operatorname{pr}\left[ x\left(k\right)\notin\mathbb{X} \right]\right]=0.17\%<1-p=5\%\). 




Lastly, although we operate close to the constraints, constraint violations are rare and the posed chance constraints (2) are met with: \(\max_{\vec{x} \in \mathbb{L}_{\geq 0}} k \, \Pr \left[ x(k) \notin \mathbb{X} \right] = 0.17\% < 1 - p = 5\%\).

Compared to common sampling-based approximations, the proposed SMPC scheme provides theoretical guarantees with an online computational complexity that is only marginally increased compared to a nominal MPC. This is crucial for implementation on embedded hardware for many applications.

IX. CONCLUSION

We presented a computationally tractable predictive control framework for nonlinear systems subject to unbounded stochastic noise. The resulting closed-loop system ensures recursive feasibility, chance constraint satisfaction, and an expected cost bound. The design leverages stochastic contraction metrics to design probabilistic reachable sets. We highlighted advantages of the proposed method in a numerical example involving nonlinear dynamics and unbounded stochastic noise. Future work aims at designing less conservative probabilistic reachable sets by leveraging more distributional information and accounting for parametric uncertainty.

For ease of exposition, we focus on the constant parametrization $M \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ from Corollary 1 and comment on addressing state-dependent metrics $M(x)$ at the end.

Jiaqi Li, Mingyao Xing, Lin Du, and Bo Xin

Abstract—In current traffic engineering, the communication geometry and channel environment of vehicles are relevant parameters in the vehicle-to-vehicle communication process. How can vehicle-to-vehicle communication realize data-driven accurate prediction for random field functions? In this letter, the conditional random fields constructed by the vehicles based on the traditional logistic-ARMA model and machine-learner algorithm are proved to be a good approach to the predicted data characteristics for both network wide channel. Further, as for vehicle-to-road state data, the interpolation and conditional random fields prediction are proved to give more reliable predictions than the traditional neural networks. Through the numerical calculation of vehicle related road scenarios, the difference of the prediction performances between the a君的 cases and practical cases demonstrates the than quantitative conclusions. Numerical results show that in the presence of line of sight errors, the conditional random fields prediction has a advantage over the traditional neural network methods. Compared to baseline models of vehicle-tocomputer prone network (vehicle-vehicle) communication, the conditional random fields prediction can give various predictions. In given network scenarios, the predicted network wide channel characteristics show the edge of exit angle restriction and inadequate speed around exit. Also in given network scenarios, the conditional random fields prediction provide the approximately 80% accuracy. In the experimental situations, the network wide channel shows higher prediction accuracy with the condition that the vehicle-obstacle space range request is greater than 30m. In the real existing risks case, the conditional random fields models can improve the sample prediction accuracy, reduce the number of predictive measurements and improve the tractability of real-world vehicles
